p: Pavel turned up in the lobby with a crate of adapters he'd built over two weekends, and the team turned it into real changes instead.
Tamarack will rebuild the rack to plug into HEARTH, and ICD revision B, signed on a workbench in Frederick, matched on all four lines.
The rack now reaches FRO in week twenty six, and Tiago will build around a steel stand-in until it does.
Amara's card, SIX WEEKS LATE, FOUR PEOPLE OUT, is still in Nadia's badge holder.
Driving home from Frederick, she counted thirteen weeks since she'd told her father she'd come down soon.
Frank Brooks. Nadia's father. He toured the high bay with one hand pocketed.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. He still tells the 2019 hatch seal story.
Odette. Safety engineer. She writes HEARTH's hazard reports.
Jun Takeda. Keeps the model, and timed how long the notices waited.
Amara Osei. Program manager. She told four hundred people six weeks.
Tiago Ferreira. Test lead. He's building around a stand-in rack.
Helen Cho-Ramirez. Halo's crew lead. She signed a priced change for ground commands.

Her father, Frank, called Sunday night, a little after eight. That was when she called Callie now. The noon alarm hadn't lasted, but the call mostly had, and Callie put Rosie on and handed the phone to him last if he was still up. Tonight he called first.

On Saturday Nadia had texted him a photo from the test cell: HEARTH's forward hatch bolted to Tiago's stand, bare aluminum with blue tape on its edges, the first piece of the module that looked like it was going to space. He hadn't texted back. He had it open now. She could tell, because he talked the way he read the paper, a few words and then a stop.
That black ring. Around the door. That rubber?
Silicone. It's the seal for the hatch.
Fifteen years, she told him. HEARTH was built for fifteen. I didn't ask about the can, he said. I asked about the ring.
She didn't know. She said Brannock, the company that molded it, would have data. He made the noise he made at the TV when a weatherman said a front might stall.

Our gloves had a date on the cuff, he said. Stamped in. Every six months back to the shop for testing, worn or not. Rubber goes bad in a hot truck. The TV went quiet on his end. Mornings, you'd roll them up tight from the cuff, so the air's caught in the fingers, and hold them up by your ear.
Even if you'd checked them the day before?
Then especially. He stopped there. It was as close as he came, most years, to the year he quit climbing, and she knew better than to lean on it.

When he came back it was in his Rosie voice. Rosie had drawn a second door on the purple rocket, at the back, because Callie had told her Nadia was putting one in. She wants to know when you're coming to see it.
The weekend after the critical design review, Nadia said. I'll text you the date.
Text it now. She did, with him still on the line. He read it out loud and said okay. It didn't sound like the other times.

After he'd hung up she opened the photo again and spread it with two fingers until the seal filled the screen: a thin black line pressed into a groove, the only thing between the cabin and whatever was on the other side of that door on the day somebody shut it. She'd checked the hatch's drawings, its loads and its open time. She'd never once asked how old the rubber would be on the day it mattered.
Colleen's Flight Notes: what could go wrong, and what you'll do.

The radio was in. The day before her father called, Colleen took the blue and white airplane up for the first time as its owner, with Nadia in the right seat. Before she untied it she pulled a laminated card from her flight bag and went down it out loud: the ceiling and visibility she'd fly in, the crosswind she'd land in, how much sleep she'd had, how long since she'd flown this kind of airplane. Most lines had a number. Two were close today, and she said so.
The card isn't for good days, she said. It's for the day I want to go.

Risk management is the process for finding, analyzing, treating and watching risks, continually, across the whole life cycle. A risk is an uncertain event or condition that would hurt the project's objectives if it happened, and it has two parts: how likely it is and how bad it would be. Planning comes first. The program decides how it'll identify risks, the scales it'll rate them on, who owns them, how often they're reviewed and where they're kept. Identification works best from many directions at once: the architecture and its interfaces, requirements that are hard to meet, suppliers, hazard analyses, lessons from earlier programs, and the people closest to the work. Write each risk with a cause and a consequence: if this condition holds, then this could happen, and here's what it would cost. "Seals are a concern" is a worry. A statement is something you can handle.
How the exam asks it. Risk management runs continually, not once. Plan the approach first, identify from many sources, and write each risk as a cause and a consequence.

Colleen's card had a small grid in one corner, four squares by four. Down the side, how likely. Across the bottom, how bad. Ice is unlikely today, she said, tapping the worst column. It's also the one that kills you. So it still gets a look.

Analysis rates each risk on likelihood and consequence, on scales the program defined up front, with words and numbers behind each level so two people rating the same risk land in the same square. Consequence is the worst credible outcome across the areas that matter: cost, schedule, technical performance and, on a crewed system, safety. Likelihood comes from evidence where there is any: test data, history, and the gaps in what's known. The ratings place the risk on a matrix, and the matrix sorts attention. Where there's a cost estimate, risk exposure puts a number on it: probability times impact. A 30 percent chance of a $500,000 hit is an exposure of $150,000. Record the basis for every rating. A score with no basis can't be argued with, and it can't be updated either.

Much of that evidence comes from system analysis, the process that turns data into the assessments risk and decision management depend on. When the data runs out before the need does, the analysis should say so plainly, not stretch the trend to fit.
How the exam asks it. Rate on defined scales and record the basis. Consequence is the worst credible outcome across cost, schedule, performance and safety. Exposure is probability times impact.
Ice was the one she had a plan for. The freezing level was well above the route, and if the cloud tops climbed she'd turn around at the reservoir. She named the reservoir before they taxied.

Handling comes in four kinds. Avoid a risk by changing the plan so it can't happen: don't fly into cloud. Mitigate it by lowering the likelihood or the consequence: more data, a better design, a backup ready. Transfer it to a party better placed to carry it, such as an insurer, or a supplier through the agreement. Transfer moves who pays. It doesn't change what happens. Accept it on purpose when handling would cost more than it saves, and keep watching. A risk that's accepted, or too uncertain to rate yet, often becomes a watch item with a trigger that brings it back for action. Every risk gets an owner, and the owner is a person, not a department.

A burn-down plan lays the handling steps out in time: each step's date and cost, and the rating the risk should drop to if the step works. Plotted against the weeks, it shows whether handling is keeping pace. When a step fails, the line goes up, and that's information too. When a risk actually happens, it stops being a risk and becomes an issue, worked through project assessment and control. The same process covers the upside. An opportunity is an uncertain event that would help if it happened, and it's managed the same way: an owner, the benefit, what has to be true, and a trigger that says when to act or let it go.

Risk management takes in candidate risks and opportunities from every other process: requirements that will be hard to meet, architecture and interface concerns, supplier status, hazard analyses, measurement trends and lessons from earlier programs. It puts out the risk management strategy, the risk profile with each item's rating, owner and handling, the treatment plans, and risk reports. Project assessment and control uses the profile to see whether handling is keeping pace and to start corrective action. Decision management uses it to weigh options. Project planning puts the handling steps into the schedule and the budget.

How the exam asks it. Avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept. Transfer shifts the cost, not the consequence. A risk that occurs becomes an issue. An opportunity gets an owner and a trigger, just like a threat. The risk profile feeds assessment and control, decisions and planning.

Climbing out of Erie, Colleen kept glancing at the temperature and the dew point. Seven degrees apart on the ground, five over Boulder. When those two close up, the fog comes, she said. The fog's the result. The spread is the warning.

Measurement sorts indicators into two kinds. A lagging indicator reports what has already happened: defects found, money spent, tests failed. A leading indicator shows a trend early enough to act on, such as a margin shrinking month by month, handling actions slipping past their dates, or a supplier's lot data creeping toward a limit while every lot still passes. INCOSE and its partners publish a guide to systems engineering leading indicators. Each indicator gets a threshold set short of the limit, so it fires while there's still room to move.

Measurement starts from information needs: what the people deciding have to know, and by when. From those it puts out a measurement strategy, the measures with their definitions and thresholds, the collected data, and measurement reports. Project assessment and control and decision management use them most, and the same trends feed the risk profile.

Earned value is a common way to read cost and schedule progress together. It rests on a work breakdown structure, the tree of all the project's work, with a budget and a date on each piece. Planned value is the budgeted cost of the work scheduled to be done by now. Earned value is the budgeted cost of the work actually done. Actual cost is what that work really cost. Those three are base measures, counted straight from the books. The indices are derived measures, worked out from them. The schedule performance index is earned value divided by planned value, and the cost performance index is earned value divided by actual cost. Below 1.0 means behind schedule, or over cost. If $90,000 of work was planned by today, $80,000 worth is done, and it cost $100,000, the schedule index is about 0.89 and the cost index is 0.80. One month's index is a lagging number. Its trend, month over month, is the leading one.
On the way back Colleen pointed out the fields she'd use if the engine stopped, one after another, without being asked.

That's resilience, one of the quality characteristics: the ability to keep providing required capability when something goes wrong, by anticipating it, withstanding it and recovering from it. Reliability tries to keep the failure from happening. Resilience plans for the day it happens anyway.

Colleen owned one airplane now, and every dollar for it came out of the same account as everything else. Portfolio management makes that call for a company: which projects to start, keep, change or stop, given its strategy and the people, facilities and money it has. A new project that needs the same people and the same test cell as a current one is a portfolio question before it's a sales question. Portfolio management takes in the organization's strategy, the business cases for proposed work and the status of the projects already running. It puts out decisions to start, keep, change or stop projects, and the resources each one gets. Project planning starts from those decisions. And people raise risks where it's safe to. A team that thanks whoever brings bad news early hears it early.

How the exam asks it. Leading indicators warn while there's time to act. Lagging indicators confirm what happened. Resilience covers withstanding and recovering, not only preventing failure. Earned value: the schedule index is earned value over planned value, the cost index is earned value over actual cost, and below 1.0 is behind or over. Portfolio management weighs projects against strategy and shared resources.

Monday of week fifteen Nadia opened HEARTH's risk register. Amara had started it on the program's first day. It had thirty one lines, most of them cost and schedule, and eleven had no owner. The newest was two months old, with one exception.
The exception was the aft node, Nadia's own line from a month back, sitting at watch with its trigger untouched: Halo's next assembly plan not showing the node.

Osprey, a company building a smaller station, had asked for proposals on a habitat module. FRO's board would decide in two weeks whether to bid, and Amara wanted HEARTH's register current before the board looked at it. There was nothing on it about the hatch. Before she did anything else she typed one line of her own, the question her father had asked on Sunday: if the seal compound ages faster than its data shows, then the hatch may not hold its leak rate late in the module's life. Owner, N. Brooks. Then she looked at the other thirty one. How does Nadia find what's missing?
A. Copy over the risk list from FRO's last cargo program and edit from there.
B. Ask Amara which risks the board will look for and make sure they're listed.
C. Walk the leads through the architecture one interface at a time.
D. Email each lead for their top five risks by Friday and merge the replies.

It takes Monday afternoon. They go element by element, then interface by interface, with Odette's hazard reports open and Wes's old programs on the table. Fourteen new lines go up, each written as if this, then that. At the hatch Wes reads her line off the screen and says the compound has flown for twenty years. She leaves it up.

That's the one. Risk identification draws on many sources together: architecture and interfaces, requirements, hazard analyses, suppliers, lessons learned and the people doing the work. Writing each risk as a cause and a consequence makes it something you can handle.

Tuesday a test cell technician named Gus caught Nadia at the coffee urn. He'd been at FRO since the cargo days, and he'd read Nadia's seal line on the HEARTH room screen Monday, on his way through with a cart. His was one of the six names on the lockout tags by the cell's valve panel. He waited until the urn was empty.

That 2019 seal, he said. Wes tells it like he caught a bad seal. He did. He also put it in. We'd bought seals for two modules and the second one got canceled, so the spare sat in a bag in the cage for two years. Wes used it because it was there. He refilled his cup. I wasn't going to say that with him at the table.
Gus has given Nadia the 2019 seal's history at the coffee urn. What should she do with it?
A. Ask Gus if she can log it under his name, then tell Wes before it goes up.
B. Log the shelf life risk with no name on it, and keep Gus out of it.
C. Leave the 2019 story off the register as history from the cargo days.
D. Thank Gus and ask him to bring it up himself at Thursday's review.

She asks Gus if she can put his name on it. He says fine, as long as she tells Wes herself. Nadia goes to Wes's desk before lunch and tells him what she's adding and who it came from. Wes looks at the 2019 photo over his desk for a while. It was my call to buy for two, he says. Put it on. At Thursday's review the leads speak last, and Gus and two other technicians add three lines before Wes says anything.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Teams surface risks when raising them is safe and normal. Crediting the source, telling the person it touches directly and with respect, and changing how meetings run all build that culture. That's systems engineering in practice, not a side issue.

Wednesday they rated the new lines. FRO's scales were Amara's, from the first day, and they were good ones: five levels each, a probability band behind every likelihood, and a cost, a schedule slip, a performance loss and a crew safety effect behind every consequence.

The seal took longest. Brannock Seal, in Ohio, had molded the compound for twenty years, and its published aging data covered the equivalent of ten. HEARTH was built for fifteen. One FRO seal had failed before, after two years in a bag. If the seal let go in the module's later years, the hatch wouldn't hold when the crew needed it shut. Finding that out on the ground meant new seals, both hatches reworked and the testing done again.
Likelihood one, Wes said. It's flown for twenty years.
Amara's five level scales are ready for the new lines. How should the seal be rated?
A. Rate the consequence on cost, and leave crew safety to the hazard reports.
B. Rate it on the scales from all the evidence, the ten year data gap included.
C. Rate it on the scales, and take likelihood from the compound's flight record.
D. Record Wes's rating of one, on the strength of his twenty years of seal flights.

Likelihood three: data for ten of fifteen years, and one failure of the same kind at FRO. Consequence four: a hatch that fails its leak rate means rework and retest, and a hatch that won't hold when it's needed. Nadia writes the basis under both numbers. Wes reads it standing, with his arms folded. You put a three on my hatch, the board sees it in yellow a week before they vote on a second module, he says. And that 2019 seal was a bag in a cage. It wasn't the rubber. Then the bag's on the cage, Nadia says. The three's on the ten years. Brannock's data stops at ten, and we're building for fifteen. That part isn't about 2019. Wes looks at the screen a long time. Then he takes the pencil from behind his ear and initials the basis line, small, the way he initials drawings he didn't draw.

Exactly right. Analysis rates each risk on the program's defined scales, from the evidence available, with its gaps named. Consequence is the worst credible outcome across cost, schedule, performance and safety, and the basis is recorded so the rating can be checked and updated.

Thursday the seal came back to the HEARTH room with a rating on it and four ideas. Wes wanted to stop worrying about rubber altogether. Amara wanted Brannock to own it. Odette wanted the risk lower before anyone called it handled. Lower first, she said. Then we can use the word.

Tiago pointed out that the hatch would be leak tested twice before it shipped, once in qualification and once as flight hardware, and that a bad seal would show. Nadia felt the pull of that one. Two leak tests. Two green passes.
The rated seal risk is back with four ways to handle it. Which should Nadia choose?
A. Accept it, with the two hatch leak tests before ship as the check.
B. Transfer it with a clause making Brannock pay for any seal that fails early.
C. Mitigate it by aging samples of HEARTH's own lot to the full fifteen years.
D. Avoid it by switching both hatches to a metal seal that doesn't age.

Brannock agrees to age samples from HEARTH's lot to a fifteen year equivalent, with results in week twenty four. Its routine aging test on the same lot ends sooner, the day after the board votes. Jun finds a second compound from another maker and orders samples. Odette signs off on the plan, not the risk.
That's the one. Mitigation lowers the likelihood, the consequence, or both. Here the long aging test closes the gap in the data, and a qualified backup shortens recovery if the seal fails.

Monday of week sixteen Jun pulled Brannock's certificates for the compound's last four lots from receiving. Each showed the same test. Samples were aged in an oven, squeezed flat for a set time, then measured for how much they failed to spring back. That was compression set, and Brannock's limit was 25 percent. HEARTH's own lot, molded the week before, was in Brannock's oven now. Its result would come at the end of next week.
Brannock Seal certificates, last four lots. Compression set after aging, oldest to newest: 14, 16, 19 and 22 percent. Limit 25 percent. All four PASS.
Brannock's lots read 14, 16, 19 and 22 percent against a 25 percent limit. What should Jun's chart show?
A. Plot each lot's measured value with an action threshold below the limit.
B. Track the hatch leak rate in qualification as the measure of the seal.
C. Track seal deliveries against the integration schedule, lot by lot.
D. Chart each lot as a pass or a fail against Brannock's 25 percent limit.

Jun plots the four points and draws the limit across the top. Nadia sets the threshold at 20 percent, where there's still room to act. The last lot is already past it. She writes to Brannock that afternoon and asks what changed. Brannock's quality manager answers that every lot passed. She asks again.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. A leading indicator shows a trend early enough to act on. Tracking the measured value against a threshold short of the limit turns a column of passes into a warning while there's time.
Tuesday Jun put the seal's line up on the screen in the HEARTH room. Its number on the register was R-032.

R-032 on the risk register, the hatch seal. If the seal compound ages faster than its ten years of data show, then both hatches may not hold their leak rate late in the module's fifteen year life. Nadia owns it, at likelihood 3 and consequence 4. The basis is ten years of aging data, one earlier FRO seal that failed in 2019 after two years in storage, and Brannock's lot results trending up.

The handling Odette had signed off on had three dated steps: Brannock's routine result on HEARTH's lot at the end of next week, a qualified backup compound a few weeks after that, and the fifteen year aging result in week twenty four.
Amara wants the date it goes green, Jun said. I told her I'd ask you, so she'd stop asking me.
R-032 is up on the HEARTH room screen. How should its handling be followed over time?
A. List each handling step with an owner and a due date, and report progress.
B. Give it one milestone, seal qualified by the review, and rate it again then.
C. Lower the rating one step a month as the team's confidence in it grows.
D. Plot the rating each step should reach by its date, then track actuals.

Jun draws it from today's score: one step for each dated action, each down to the rating it should reach if it works, and a second line for what really happens. Amara looks for the week it goes green. And if a step fails? Then the line goes up, and we see it the week it does.

Exactly right. A burn-down plan ties each handling step to a date and the rating it should reach, so progress shows against the plan. A failed step shows up as the line rising, which is exactly when action is needed.
Wednesday Tiago drove up to Frederick for the first monthly review on Tamarack's floor. Irena walked him to the whiteboard at the end of the clean room. She'd moved the magnets herself.
He came back with a photo. Eight of the twenty packages were green. The forecast from two weeks back, two a week, said nine by now.
The integration plan Amara had signed still read the same: Tamarack's stand-in first, the real rack three weeks later, and the ship date moving only if the rack slipped past week twenty eight.
Amara saw the photo before Nadia did. One package behind, she said. Do I call Pavel?
Tiago's photo shows eight of twenty packages green, and the forecast said nine. What should Nadia do?
A. Have Tamarack send a recovery plan for the missed package by Friday.
B. Forecast the finish against the chamber date, and log the variance.
C. Re-baseline the plan to today's count and rate, and work to that.
D. Ask Tamarack for a weekend shift until the count is back on forecast.

Nadia works it with Amara over the photo. Twelve left at two a week, so Tamarack finishes about two weeks before its test chamber frees up. The chamber's the real clock. The rack still lands in week twenty six, with about a week and a half of float, and that's nowhere near the trigger. She logs the variance and the float. Amara doesn't call Pavel.

That's the one. Assessment compares progress with the plan and forecasts from it. Control acts when a variance crosses a set threshold or threatens what matters. Recording a variance that doesn't is part of control too.
Thursday Tiago called her down to the test cell. He had the cell's schedule on the whiteboard by the valve panel, where the six lockout tags still hung.

The week after next, the forward hatch's qualification article went into the chamber for its leak test: three days to pump down, hold and measure, and bring it back up. Three weeks after that the seal fixture went in for its own leak test, a steel ring with the hatch's groove cut into it, and that was three more days. After that the cell was booked solid with the aft hatch.

The fixture fits on the hatch stand, he said. He'd already measured it. Same chamber, same helium, separate lines so the two leaks don't mix. One pumpdown. I get three days back, and I don't burn a second helium charge. The fixture has to be built and leak checked by the end of next week, or it doesn't work.
The hatch and the seal fixture are booked weeks apart in the cell. How should Nadia handle Tiago's idea?
A. Log it as an opportunity with Tiago as owner and a go or no go date.
B. Tell Tiago to go ahead and build the fixture on his own schedule.
C. Keep the two tests separate in the cell schedule, as already planned.
D. Combine them, and shorten the hatch's hold from a day to half a day.

She writes it with him at the whiteboard. Opportunity: shared pumpdown. Owner: Tiago. Benefit: three days of cell time and a helium charge. Must be true: the fixture built and leak checked by Friday of next week, separate measurement lines, and both procedures still meeting their own objectives. Trigger: if the fixture isn't ready that Friday, both tests run separately as planned. Tiago initials it. I'd have done it anyway, he says. Now I'll know when to stop.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Risk management covers opportunities as well as threats. An opportunity gets the same treatment: an owner, the expected benefit, the conditions it depends on, and a trigger for when to act or let it go.
Friday Helen called about the seal. Halo's crew office read every hazard report FRO sent, and Odette's report for losing hatch isolation now pointed at the seal.
The day that seal matters is the day somebody shuts that hatch because something's wrong on one side of it, Helen said. Suppose it's tired by then. Year twelve, say. What does my crew do?

Nadia started to answer, and Helen kept going, slower now. The night of the galley fire, when the last one got to the node, the commander shut the hatch behind them. It held fourteen minutes, till the air cleared. I've got both times in my wallet. The line hissed a little. I can tell you the minute that hatch shut. I couldn't tell you the year that seal was made. Nobody on console could. We were all watching the clock.
After the call Nadia opened the photo of the forward hatch again. Her father had skipped the can and gone straight to the ring.
Odette's hatch isolation report now points at the seal, and Halo reads every one. What should FRO plan?
A. Specify a seal rated for twenty years, past the module's design life.
B. Plan how the crew would find a weak seal and change it from the inside.
C. Put two seals in series in the hatch groove, each a backup for the other.
D. Plan to fly a spare seal up on a supply flight if the crew reports a leak.

It turns into three things. A leak check the crew can run across the shut hatch in ten minutes. A procedure for keeping the hatch shut on a weak seal while the station tops up the air. And a spare seal on board with its tools, so the crew can change it from the cabin side, which Wes says he can design for if he knows now. Helen asks for the ten minutes in writing.

Exactly right. Resilience is the ability to keep providing required capability when something goes wrong. Planning how the crew detects the problem, withstands it and recovers from it covers what prevention alone can't.
Decision ten. What the board sees.

Monday of week seventeen Amara came to Nadia's desk with a note from Margaret Doyle, who chaired FRO's board. Osprey's request was real: one habitat module for a smaller station, proposals due in five weeks. The board would vote on Thursday. Before it voted, the chair wanted to know whether HEARTH was healthy enough to bet a second module on, and she'd asked for one number: the count of red risks.
I've stood on that crate with bad news once this year, Amara said. I'd like to stand on it and say we're bidding on something.
The board chair wants one number before the vote, the count of red risks. What should Nadia give her?
A. Give the board HEARTH's percent complete and its cost to date each month.
B. Give the board the whole register and let it judge HEARTH's health itself.
C. Give the board the count of red and yellow risks each month, with its trend.
D. Give the board a few leading indicators, each with its own threshold.

Nadia gives Amara four lines instead of a count, each with a threshold: the burn-down of each top risk against its plan, the share of handling actions done on time, the predicted egress margins, and Tamarack's packages against forecast. Amara stops at the second line and asks which of these would have warned her about the rack. Actions on time. Pavel's would have been late by week ten. Amara is quiet a moment. I'd have liked week ten.

That's the one. Leading indicators show trends early enough to act on, with thresholds set ahead of the limits. They answer the board's real need, whether the program will stay healthy, better than a count of today's reds.
Tuesday Amara built the board's deck. HEARTH's five highest risks went on one slide. At a twelve, the seal was one of the five.
Wes came in while she was arranging it. Brannock's result on our lot comes Friday, he said. If it passes, the seal comes off that slide. Don't put my hatch in front of the board for three days.
Amara looked at Nadia. It would be one meeting with good news in it, she said. She didn't say it like an order.
Brannock's result on HEARTH's lot comes the day after the vote. How should the seal appear in the deck?
A. Lead the slide with the seal, shown in red, ahead of the other four.
B. Keep it on the register, but move it from the slide to the deck's backup pages.
C. Show it on the slide as rated, with Friday's test date and what failure costs.
D. Keep the seal on Wes's own list until Friday, off the register the board sees.

The seal stays on the slide, one line, the same as on the register: the rating, the handling, the result due Friday, and the cost if the lot fails. Wes reads it without a word. An hour later he sends Nadia the 2019 leak report, scanned, with no note.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Risk management communicates the risk profile, as it stands, to the people who decide. A risk with a test result days away is shown with that date and both outcomes, so the decision can account for either.

The board met Thursday afternoon in the conference room over the lobby: seven people, Amara at the screen, and Nadia on a seat by the wall, because the chair of the board had asked for HEARTH's systems engineer by title.

Osprey wanted a module like HEARTH, a little smaller, in two years. Building it would need FRO's high bay, its test cell and the people who had built HEARTH so far, while HEARTH was still being built.
The chair stopped on the risk slide, at the seal. Friday, she said. And if it fails? Amara told her what it would cost.

The chair had a pen she never wrote with. She set it down square to the edge of the table. My father ran a press on the floor under this room, she said. Streetlight housings, back when the sign out front was true. The year I started high school, Centennial Lighting took a second big order on the same line, with the same people, and couldn't make either one on time. It lost both. Three hundred families heard on a Friday afternoon. Nobody at the table moved. Amara had told Nadia once that the chair never talked about the lighting company. Now Nadia knew why she'd asked for one number. So I'd like a straight answer.
Then the board's chair looked past Amara to Nadia. Ms. Brooks. Can FRO build two of these at once?
Osprey's module needs FRO's high bay, test cell and HEARTH's people. What should Nadia tell the board?
A. Recommend that FRO bid, and staff it from HEARTH's team as people free up.
B. Leave the bid to Amara and the rest of the board as a business question.
C. Recommend that FRO wait and bid on the next module once HEARTH ships.
D. Lay out what a second module would share with HEARTH, and when.

Nadia does it in four minutes. Wes and Tiago can't move before HEARTH's critical design review, the test cell is full through week thirty, and a bid could reuse HEARTH's design and start from its risk register. The board votes to bid, with its own team, HEARTH first in the test cell, and a go or no go before the proposal goes out. When the vote is done Nadia takes the card out of her badge holder, SIX WEEKS LATE, FOUR PEOPLE OUT, and slides it down the table. Amara writes the three conditions on the back and hands it back to her.

Exactly right. Portfolio management starts, sustains, redirects or ends projects to fit the organization's strategy and capacity. A sound bid decision weighs the shared people, facilities and risks, and sets conditions that protect the work already under way.
Brannock's email came in at twenty to four on Friday.

An email from Brannock Seal, Quality. Subject: Lot hold, HEARTH hatch seal compound. Nadia, Wes, The lot molded for HEARTH failed lot acceptance today. After accelerated aging, compression set was 31 percent against our 25 percent limit. Retained samples retested at 30 percent. The lot is on hold, including both hatch seals, the two spares, and the two fixture samples we sent early for fit. We're looking at what changed in our process this year. You'll have first findings next week. Brannock Quality

Amara forwarded it to the board's chair within ten minutes, with two lines of her own: the seal result we discussed yesterday, failed; handling under way, cost and schedule by Wednesday. The chair answered from her phone. Understood. The bid conditions stand.

Nadia went down to the test cell. Tiago had the seal fixture on the bench beside the hatch stand, finished and leak checked that morning for Monday's pumpdown, a steel ring with a black seal pressed into its groove. The trigger on his opportunity had a date on it, and the date was today. The fixture was ready. The seal wasn't.
She read the lot number off the traveler tag wired to the fixture and checked it against the email. Same lot as both flight seals, still sitting in Ohio.

Tiago opened the drawer under the valve panel, where the lockout tags were kept, and took out a red one printed HOLD. He wrote the lot number on it and held out the pen. It's your line on the register, he said. Same rule as the lockouts. Your name goes on it, and only you take it off. She wrote her name.
Under it she wrote the date, the way the date had been stamped on her father's gloves. She hung the tag on the fixture's valve and squared it on its wire.

Wes came down while she was doing it. He looked at the tag. Then he ran his thumb around the seal in its groove, all the way around, the way he'd seated every one he ever put in. In 2019 I put mine in myself, and I found it the week it shipped, he said. This is week seventeen. He went back up the stairs. A minute later she could hear him on the phone to Ohio.

Upstairs she changed the seal's line on the register from a risk to an issue, and Jun's burn-down redrew itself. The step down that was due this week went the other way. The line went up the week it happened, the way she'd told Amara it would.
